title: Moment of Inertia of a Sphere
short_intro: The moment of inertia of a sphere measures its rotational inertia about a given axis passing through its geometric centre or tangent. For a solid sphere of mass M and radius R, the moment of inertia about a diametrical axis is (2/5)MR², while for a thin spherical shell it is (2/3)MR².

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of moment of inertia of solid and hollow spheres (spherical shells) about a diameter, and direct application of parallel and perpendicular axis theorems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of moment of inertia using spherical polar volume/surface elements, integration techniques for variable density spheres, and rolling dynamics on inclined planes.

prerequisites: Definition and physical significance of moment of inertia (I = ∫ r² dm)
Parallel axis theorem and Perpendicular axis theorem
Integration techniques for continuous mass distributions

concept_notes.heading: Moment of Inertia of a Thin Spherical Shell
bullets: Consider a thin spherical shell of mass M and radius R. The mass is distributed entirely on the surface.
Choosing a ring element of thickness R d(θ) at an angle θ from the axis of rotation, its radius is r = R sin(θ) and its mass is dm = (M / 4πR²) * (2πR sin(θ) R d(θ)).
Integrating the elemental moment of inertia dI = dm (R sin(θ))² over θ from 0 to π yields I = (2/3)MR².

concept_notes.heading: Moment of Inertia of a Solid Sphere
bullets: A solid sphere of mass M and radius R can be viewed as an assembly of concentric thin spherical shells of varying radii r and thickness dr.
The mass of a shell of radius r and thickness dr is dm = (M / ((4/3)πR³)) * 4πr² dr = (3M / R³) r² dr.
Integrating the moment of inertia of each shell dI = (2/3) dm r² from r = 0 to r = R yields the standard result I = (2/5)MR².

concept_notes.heading: Moment of Inertia about a Tangent Axis
bullets: Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a tangent to a solid sphere is I_tangent = I_diameter + M(R)² = (2/5)MR² + MR² = (7/5)MR².
For a thin spherical shell, the tangent moment of inertia is I_tangent = (2/3)MR² + MR² = (5/3)MR².
This theorem is valid for any parallel shift of the axis from the centre of mass to the boundary.

concept_notes.heading: Radius of Gyration for Spheres
bullets: The radius of gyration k is defined by the relation I = Mk².
For a solid sphere about a diameter, k = sqrt(2/5) R.
For a thin spherical shell about a diameter, k = sqrt(2/3) R.

derivations.title: Derivation of Moment of Inertia of a Thin Spherical Shell
derivations.conditions: Thin hollow sphere of mass M, radius R, rotating about its diametrical axis.
steps: Take a ring element on the shell surface at polar angle θ having width R d(θ).
The radius of this circular ring about the z-axis is y = R sin(θ).
The mass of the ring is dm = (M / 4πR²) * (2πR sin(θ)) * (R d(θ)) = (M / 2) sin(θ) d(θ).
The moment of inertia of this ring is dI = dm y² = (M / 2) sin(θ) * (R^2 sin^2(θ)) d(θ) = (MR^2 / 2) sin^3(θ) d(θ).
Integrate from θ = 0 to π: I = (MR^2 / 2) ∫_{0}^{pi} sin^3(θ) d(θ) = (2/3) MR^2.

derivations.title: Derivation of Moment of Inertia of a Solid Sphere
derivations.conditions: Solid sphere of uniform density, mass M, radius R, rotating about its diameter.
steps: Divide the solid sphere into concentric thin spherical shells of radius r and infinitesimal thickness dr.
Volume of a spherical shell is dV = 4πr² dr.
Mass of the shell is dm = ρ dV = (M / ((4/3)πR^3)) * 4πr^2 dr = (3M / R^3) r^2 dr.
The moment of inertia of this individual shell about its diameter is dI = (2/3) dm r^2 = (2/3) * ((3M / R^3) r^2 dr) * r^2 = (2M / R^3) r^4 dr.
Integrate from r = 0 to r = R: I = ∫_{0}^{R} (2M / R^3) r^4 dr = (2M / R^3) * [R^5 / 5] = (2/5) MR^2.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Torsional Pendulum Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic of a sphere suspended by a vertical wire, showing angular oscillation.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The period of oscillation T = 2π sqrt(I / C) where C is the torsional rigidity of the wire. Measuring T allows experimental determination of I.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked conceptual questions relating oscillation period to mass distribution and moment of inertia.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Rolling Sphere on Inclined Plane
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An inclined plane at angle θ with a sphere rolling down without slipping.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Acceleration depends on the moment of inertia: a = (g sin(θ)) / (1 + (I / (M R^2))). Solid sphere accelerates faster than a hollow shell.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in numericals comparing linear and rotational accelerations of various rolling bodies.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Mass Distribution vs. MOI Comparative Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bar chart or curve showing I / (M R^2) values for a ring (1.0), hollow sphere (0.67), solid cylinder (0.5), solid sphere (0.4).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Greater concentration of mass away from the rotation axis results in a higher moment of inertia coefficient.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct factual multiple-choice questions in TGT/PGT exams.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the moment of inertia of a solid sphere of mass 5 kg and radius 0.2 m about a diametrical axis.
solution_steps: Identify the formula for a solid sphere about a diameter: I = (2/5) M R^2.
Substitute the given values: M = 5 kg, R = 0.2 m.

solved_numericals.question: Find the moment of inertia of a thin spherical shell of mass 3 kg and radius 0.5 m about a tangent to its surface.
solution_steps: Identify the formula for a thin spherical shell about a tangent: I = (5/3) M R^2.
Substitute M = 3 kg and R = 0.5 m.

solved_numericals.question: A solid sphere of mass 2 kg and radius 0.1 m rolls without slipping down an inclined plane of height 2 m. Find its translational velocity when it reaches the bottom.
solution_steps: Apply conservation of mechanical energy: Potential Energy at top = Translational Kinetic Energy + Rotational Kinetic Energy at bottom.
For a solid sphere, I = (2/5) M R^2 and ω = v / R, so (1/2) I ω^2 = (1/2) * ((2/5) M R^2) * (v^2 / R^2) = (1/5) M v^2.
Equate to M g h: M g h = (7/10) M v^2 => v = sqrt((10/7) g h).
Substitute g = 9.8 m/s^2, h = 2 m: v = sqrt((10 / 7) * 9.8 * 2) = sqrt(28) ≈ 5.29 m/s.

assumptions_and_limitations: The density of the sphere is assumed to be uniform unless stated otherwise as a function of radius.
Rigid body approximation is assumed; deformations or vibrational modes during rotation are neglected.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The moment of inertia of a solid sphere and a spherical shell of the same mass and radius are both equal to (2/3)MR².
common_misconceptions.correct: A solid sphere has MOI of (2/5)MR² while a spherical shell has (2/3)MR².
common_misconceptions.why: Mass distribution in a solid sphere is spread throughout the volume, bringing more mass closer to the axis of rotation compared to a shell.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Moment of inertia is a constant intrinsic property independent of the choice of axis.
common_misconceptions.correct: Moment of inertia depends heavily on the orientation, position, and choice of the axis of rotation.
common_misconceptions.why: The distance r of mass elements from the rotation axis changes with the axis location.

quick_revision: Solid sphere diameter MOI is (2/5)MR²; tangent MOI is (7/5)MR².
Spherical shell diameter MOI is (2/3)MR²; tangent MOI is (5/3)MR².
